summary: This informational document specifies how TI-LFA mechanisms can be used with Multicast-only Fast Reroute (MoFRR) for PIM. Because TI-LFA precomputes backup paths that avoid failures, it can help multicast streams recover quickly from link or node failures.

plainLanguage.summary: A live video can be sent along a spare route as well, so if one road breaks the picture keeps going. This document explains how to pick good spare routes.

subtitle: Using topology-independent backup paths for fast multicast rerouting.

tldr.problem: RFC 7431 specifies Multicast-Only Fast Reroute (MoFRR) using Loop-Free Alternates (LFA) to quickly reroute multicast traffic when a link fails. However, conventional LFA has limitations in certain network topologies and cannot provide backup paths for all destinations, leaving some multicast flows vulnerable.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC shows how to use Topology Independent LFA (TI-LFA) as the basis for MoFRR backup paths. TI-LFA precomputes backup paths that are independent of topology and offers broader coverage. By embedding the TI-LFA backup path information into PIM Join messages using RPF Vector attributes, multicast backup trees can be established hop-by-hop along the TI-LFA paths.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now provide fast reroute protection for multicast traffic in network topologies where conventional MoFRR does not work. The approach is optional and backward compatible.

facts.label: Multicast protocol changes
facts.value: None; uses existing RPF Vector attributes

facts.label: Backward compatibility
facts.value: Fully compatible; routers not supporting RPF Vectors simply ignore them

facts.label: Network topology dependency
facts.value: Independent; TI-LFA works across diverse topologies

today: RFC 9860 is an Informational RFC representing IETF consensus. It is not a standard but provides guidance for implementing TI-LFA-based multicast fast reroute. The approach is optional and can be deployed in networks using Segment Routing where multicast protection is needed and conventional LFA is insufficient.

sections.title: Multicast Fast Reroute and Its Limitations
sections.content:
Multicast is the transmission of data to many receivers at once using one data stream. If a link breaks in a multicast network, all traffic along that link is lost until the routing protocol reconverges, which takes time.

Multicast-Only Fast Reroute (MoFRR, defined in RFC 7431) reduces this loss by precomputing a secondary path. If the primary path fails, traffic switches immediately to the secondary path while the network converges.

The RFC uses Loop-Free Alternates (LFA) to find the secondary path. However, LFA has a fundamental limitation: it depends on the network topology. In certain topology patterns, no LFA exists even when alternate paths do. This means MoFRR cannot protect some multicast flows, leaving holes in the protection.
sections.plainLanguage: When a video stream is sent over a network, losing the main connection loses the stream. The network can prepare a backup route to switch to instantly. But finding a good backup route is not always possible depending on how the network is wired.

sections.title: Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate
sections.content:
Topology Independent LFA (TI-LFA, defined in RFC 9855) is a technique that computes backup paths for unicast traffic that are independent of network topology. For every destination advertised by the routing protocol, TI-LFA precomputes a backup path that avoids a failing link and is ready to be activated on failure detection.

TI-LFA works with Segment Routing (SR), a method where routers are identified by Segment IDs (SIDs). The backup path is represented as a segment list: a sequence of node and link SIDs that guides traffic through the network. This segment list is computed once and stored, ready to use immediately on failure.

The key advantage of TI-LFA is that it provides much broader coverage across diverse network topologies. Unlike LFA, which fails in certain topology patterns, TI-LFA can compute a backup path for almost every destination.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of relying on the network shape to pick a backup route, a smarter algorithm pre-computes routes that work on almost any network. When a link breaks, the network already knows where to send the traffic.

sections.title: Applying TI-LFA to Multicast
sections.content:
For multicast, RFC 7761 (PIM) builds trees by sending Join messages hop-by-hop from receivers towards the source. To apply TI-LFA to multicast, this RFC explains how to incorporate the TI-LFA backup path into PIM Join messages.

The TI-LFA backup path is a segment list of node and adjacency (link) SIDs. Using existing standards (RFC 5496 and RFC 7891), these SIDs can be converted to IP addresses and embedded into PIM Join messages as RPF Vector Attributes. These attributes guide the router on which neighbor to send the Join message to at each hop along the backup path.

When a router receives a PIM Join message with RPF Vector Attributes, it follows the specified path instead of computing the standard RPF (Reverse Path Forwarding) towards the source. This allows the backup multicast tree to be built hop-by-hop along the TI-LFA path without needing to encapsulate the entire message as a unicast tunnel.

The RFC does not require any changes to PIM itself. It reuses existing RPF Vector mechanisms and is fully compatible with current implementations. If a router does not understand RPF Vectors, it simply discards them, causing that backup path to become inactive, which is safe.
sections.plainLanguage: The router marks the backup path with clues in the Join message, telling intermediate routers how to forward it. Each router looks at the clues and forwards to the next hop on the backup route.

sections.title: Operational Deployment and Management
sections.content:
This RFC introduces an optional approach for backup paths and is designed for networks using Segment Routing. Deployment requires that all routers on the backup path understand and support RPF Vector Attributes from RFC 5496 and RFC 7891.

During normal operation, both primary and secondary multicast trees exist. If the primary path fails, traffic immediately switches to the secondary tree while the network reconverges. Because the secondary tree is pre-established and tested, convergence is faster than it would be with standard routing reconvergence.

Administratively, an operator can verify that backup paths are set up correctly using traceroute tools such as Mtrace (RFC 8487) designed for multicast. The approach does not alter how LFA, TI-LFA, or Remote LFA are managed or configured; it is simply an additional application of the precomputed backup path data.
sections.plainLanguage: The backup route is computed once and ready to use. If something breaks, traffic switches immediately. Tools can check that the backup is set up correctly before a failure happens.
